title: X-ray technique advances temperature measurements under extreme pressure
excerpt: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials subjected to extreme pressures at the National Ignition Facility (NIF), providing new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high-energy-density physics.
content_html:
Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials subjected to extreme pressures at the National Ignition Facility (NIF), providing new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high-energy-density physics.

In a study published in Physical Review B, researchers compressed tantalum, a dense, heat-resistant metal, to pressures several million times greater than Earth's atmosphere. They used X-ray diffraction to determine its crystal structure and a technique called extended X-ray absorption fine structure, or EXAFS, to measure its temperature.

The experiments confirmed that tantalum retained its crystal structure at pressures exceeding 500 gigapascals and demonstrated a new way to measure the temperature of heavy elements compressed at NIF.

"Measuring temperature under these extreme conditions is extraordinarily challenging, but it's essential to understanding how materials respond," said LLNL physicist Andrew Krygier, who led the research. "These experiments give us a new way to test our models, identify sources of heating we might otherwise miss and improve our ability to predict material behavior."

A thermometer for extreme conditions

Temperature influences nearly every aspect of a material's response, including its compressibility, strength, phase stability and transport properties. Yet measuring temperature remains one of the major challenges in dynamic-compression research because the extreme conditions last only billionths of a second, and each of the few available techniques has its own challenges, limitations and uncertainties.

EXAFS provides a way to make that measurement by tracking subtle changes in how a material absorbs X-rays, revealing the distances between neighboring atoms and how much they are moving. Researchers compare the measured signal with physics-based computer calculations to determine the sample's temperature.

Because EXAFS can capture the necessary information in a single experiment, it is well suited to NIF's brief, high-pressure conditions. By measuring X-ray absorption at an element's L-edge, the approach also opens a practical path to studying heavy elements where absorption properties make them difficult to characterize using more conventional methods.

Tantalum was an important test material because its behavior under pressure has been extensively studied by LLNL and other National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) laboratories. It also remains stable across a wide range of pressures and temperatures. At the same time, tantalum heats up readily and strongly absorbs X-rays, making it a demanding test of the experimental approach.

Strength and unexpected heating

Using X-ray diffraction, researchers found that tantalum retained the same basic crystal structure at pressures exceeding 500 gigapascals, or roughly 5 million times atmospheric pressure, with no evidence of another structure that previous calculations suggested might appear under these conditions.

The temperature measurements produced another insight. At approximately 200 gigapascals, temperatures measured with EXAFS matched computer calculations only when models accounted for tantalum's strength. Because tantalum resists being compressed, some of the energy used to compress it is converted into additional heating.

At approximately 400 gigapascals, however, the sample was much hotter than the computer models predicted. Researchers found that additional heating from X-rays emitted by plasma could plausibly explain much of the difference. The plasma formed when the NIF lasers struck the target's outer beryllium layer, and the team's analysis suggests trace amounts of iron and nickel in the beryllium may have increased the X-ray emission. The extent of that effect remains uncertain.

"This result has already changed how we model the laser-plasma interaction and how we think about designing future high-pressure experiments," Krygier said.

The study builds on earlier EXAFS experiments at NIF that measured temperatures in copper. The new tantalum experiments mark the first use of L-edge EXAFS at the facility, extending the technique to heavier elements.

"L-edge EXAFS is more challenging due to smaller signals," said LLNL physicist Yuan Ping, the experimental campaign's principal investigator. "The energetic NIF laser and high-resolution diagnostic development in past years enabled these high-quality measurements."

Both the earlier copper experiments and the new tantalum study revealed unexpected sources of heating, underscoring the value of directly measuring temperature rather than relying solely on computer predictions.

Building confidence in predictive models

The findings demonstrate why independently measuring temperature is essential. If a sample is hotter than models predict, researchers could misinterpret its strength, melting behavior or changes in structure.

By providing experimental temperature measurements that can be compared to computer simulations, EXAFS helps researchers identify gaps in their models and strengthen the experimental and computational capabilities that underpin NNSA's stockpile stewardship and modernization efforts.

The tantalum work also contributes to a broader effort across the nuclear security enterprise and its research partners to validate temperature measurement techniques, with the bulk temperature measurement from EXAFS complementing surface-radiance-based methods on other platforms.

The collaboration includes LLNL, Los Alamos and Sandia national laboratories, the Nevada National Security Site, Washington State University and the University of Rochester's Laboratory for Laser Energetics.

By combining extreme-condition experiments, X-ray diagnostics, computer modeling and high-performance computing, the project provides new data to test models and improve predictions of material behavior under extreme conditions. These capabilities contribute to a broader understanding of materials at high pressures and temperatures while supporting NNSA's mission to maintain and modernize the nation's nuclear deterrent.
